Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the account consoles the Prophet over rejection and threatens his opponents."}, {"id": "79:17/q15/p2", "position": "It warns resurrection-deniers by showing humanity's final fate.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī describes the sūra's purpose as establishing resurrection and gathering after the preceding sūras' full exposition, with oaths marking a decisive climax. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the account warns polytheists whose denial of resurrection undermines religious law."}, {"id": "79:17/q15/p3", "position": "Pharaoh's destruction demonstrates Moses' authorized mission and God's lordship over people.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says destruction of Pharaoh and his army proves Moses' divine authorization, which entails God's lordship against the polytheists' claim that lesser lords govern them."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q01", "question": "What does “هل لك” convey in Moses’ address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q01/p1", "position": "It asks whether Pharaoh has a desire, need, or inclination toward the offered purification, in an established idiom of invitation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī and al-Bursevī gloss the desire or need; al-Elmalılı adds intention. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a concise fixed invitation, like asking a guest to stay, and cites Kaʿb’s هل لك فيما and Bujayr’s هل لك في التي. Al-Rāzī compares هل لك في. Al-Samīn gives هل لك في الخير as an idiom for رغبة. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the question as asking inclination."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q02", "question": "How is “هل لك إلى أن تزكى” grammatically understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the unusual إلى is explained by an omitted noun, an implicit verb of inviting, an expanded sense of the preposition, or figurative usage.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q02/p1", "position": "An implicit nominal such as need or desire supplies the omitted subject of the question.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says هل لك في ذلك, like لا عليك and من له في ذلك, omits understood حاجة through frequent use. Al-Fārisī supplies حاجة أو إربة; al-Wāḥidī gives the same and cites an anonymous poetic line. Al-Rāzī reports al-Wāḥidī and cites هل لكم فيها إلي. Al-Samīn describes لك as predicate of an omitted subject, with إلى أن attached to it, and cites the same poetic pattern. Al-Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr also identify an implicit subject, Ibn ʿĀshūr suggesting رغبة or ميل; al-Elmalılı similarly notes implied subject. Al-Ālūsī locates إلى with the omitted predicate and cites poetry, while recording others' omitted رغبة."}, {"id": "79:18/q02/p2", "position": "The implicit noun can specifically be a way or access to purification.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī allows an omitted سبيل, as does al-Samīn's paraphrase هل لك سبيل إلى التزكية; Abū Ḥayyān lists a way alongside desire and need."}, {"id": "79:18/q02/p3", "position": "The unusual “إلى” reflects an implied invitation, so the construction includes the force of ‘I call you to.’", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ explains إلى through an intended أدعوك; al-Samīn says this does not change parsing. Al-Burhān treats it as تضمين and says the prepositional phrase is governed by لك. Al-Itqān explains verbal تضمين as one verb carrying another's meaning and unusual preposition; it favors expanding the verb over the preposition because verb examples are more numerous, and applies أدعوك here. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn Jinnī's shared-meaning account via al-Ṭībī, comparing رفث إلى at 2:187; al-Ālūsī allows attachment to the utterance's meaning or an implicit expression."}, {"id": "79:18/q02/p4", "position": "“إلى” is used with the sense of the more usual “في.”", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this explanation alongside the implicit-call reading. Al-Itqān explicitly glosses إلى as في here, ‘are you willing in this matter?’ Its discussion says some linguists and grammarians favor expanding the preposition's sense."}, {"id": "79:18/q02/p5", "position": "The preposition signals a figurative invitation rather than a syntactic inclusion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this alternative to Ibn Jinnī's تضمين; al-Bursevī also allows هل لك as figurative for ‘shall I attract and invite you?’ Al-Itqān says تضمين is figurative because a word cannot literally carry both meanings simultaneously."}, {"id": "79:18/q02/p6", "position": "The object of “إلى” is elided and understood as desire, need, or a way toward something.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explicitly proposes an omitted object of إلى and cites an unnamed poet; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also says its object is elided, yielding inclination to purification."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q03", "question": "Why does Moses frame the offer as a question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q03/p1", "position": "The question offers purification gently and tactfully, drawing Pharaoh toward acceptance.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls it an invitation any reasonable person would accept. Al-Bursevī says the tactful, unthreatening offer could draw Pharaoh from obstinacy, avoiding accusations of polytheism, ignorance, or disbelief. Al-Ālūsī says it lowers Pharaoh from arrogance. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ ties its tact to 20:44. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes an encouraging offer. Al-Elmalılı says beginning with desire recognizes inclination and intention as prerequisites for voluntary acts."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q04", "question": "What purification does “تزكى” invite Pharaoh to seek?", "turns_on": "Whether purification is the initial move to faith, its declaration, good conduct, comprehensive moral growth, repentance from tyranny, inward self-effacement, or charity; the charity gloss is disputed in Pharaoh's unbelieving context.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q04/p1", "position": "To leave unbelief or shirk and embrace faith, Islam, and God's oneness.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes repairing corruption and accepting God's oneness. Al-Ṭabarī says pure belief; Ibn Zayd links this sense throughout the Qur'an to Islam, citing 20:76 and 80:3, 7. Al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī cite 91:9 and 18:74 for purification from shirk, al-Fārisī also 80:7. Al-Māwardī transmits Qatāda. Al-Baghawī says both readings indicate escape from shirk, Islam, and uprightness. Al-Rāzī says the invitation includes monotheism and religious law. Others mention rebellion, tyranny, obedience, or freeing Israel as extensions of the change."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p2", "position": "To cleanse deficiencies and vices and acquire virtues: a full moral purification that includes faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says restricting the sense to conversion or the declaration is too narrow. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Biqāʿī agree; al-Biqāʿī specifies outward and inward vices, with faith and freeing Israel as the lowest beginning. Al-Bursevī adds the opacity of human and natural conditions. Al-Elmalılı adds growth in Islamic qualities; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ adds growth of the soul's virtues. Al-Rāzī speaks of every defect and what is unfitting."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p3", "position": "To profess that there is no deity but God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports ʿIkrima. Al-Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās, and also Muqātil's related formulation of affirming divine oneness. Al-Baghawī reports Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Qurṭubī transmits it through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Qushayrī reports a promise attached to the declaration: an imperishable kingdom, ageless youth, four hundred years of comfort, then paradise. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the formula is contained in a broader purification."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p4", "position": "To do good.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Wāḥidī both report this gloss from al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p5", "position": "To repent of tyranny and return to God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this reading, with ensuing faith-driven fear motivating obedience and restraining sin."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p6", "position": "In an inward reading, to annihilate selfhood.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says guidance to fear is knowledge of the unity of the Essence, which softens and dissolves selfhood."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p7", "position": "To give alms.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr's explanation derives this from assimilated تتزكى. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Khālawayh reject applying it here because Moses first called an unbeliever to belief, not charity; Ibn Khālawayh cites the wording زكية in 18:74. Al-Qurṭubī reports Abū ʿAmr's preference for the light reading and belief sense."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q05", "question": "What lexical sense and form underlie “تزكى”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q05/p1", "position": "It draws on purity and growth in goodness; the reflexive form conveys seeking or working to become pure.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says zakāh is growth in good, zākī grows in good, and tazakkī seeks that status. Al-Rāzī takes zakī as free of defects, citing 18:74 and 91:9. Ibn ʿĀshūr says zakāt is increase, conventionally inward good without a contextual clue, citing 91:9–10; he says the reflexive form implies self-training. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says zakā is growth in goodness and blessing. Al-Elmalılı joins cleansing and flourishing."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q06", "question": "How is “تزكى” read and formed?", "turns_on": "How the original two tāʾs of تتزكى are reduced, which readers transmit each form, and whether the stronger form carries a distinct sense.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q06/p1", "position": "With a doubled zāy, assimilating a tāʾ from original تتزكى.", "reasons": "Reports assign it variously to Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr; the Hijaz readers and Yaʿqūb; Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Yaʿqūb; and in variant transmissions Abū ʿAmr. {"id": "79:18/q11", "question": "What report explains Moses' concern that Pharaoh would refuse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q11/p1", "position": "Moses asked why he should go if Pharaoh would not accept; God ordered him on, saying twelve thousand angels seek knowledge of destiny without attaining it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī attributes the report to Sakhr ibn Juwayriyya; al-Bursevī reports the same episode without that attribution in the note."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q12", "question": "How does the Pharaoh episode serve the sūra's wider argument?", "turns_on": "The notes draw either the sūra's resurrection warning through Pharaoh's failure or the proof of divine lordship and fair warning through a messenger.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q12/p1", "position": "Pharaoh's failed worldly power supports the sūra's warning about final fate and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the sūra establishes resurrection and gathering after the preceding sūras' fuller exposition; its oaths bring the matter to a climax. He says Pharaoh's reputation and projects failed to save him, citing 28:38 and 40:37, and that God reassured Moses against Pharaoh's power."}, {"id": "79:18/q12/p2", "position": "It warns resurrection-denying polytheists, consoles the Prophet, and establishes God's lordship through Moses' authorized mission.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Pharaoh's destruction proves Moses' divine authorization, which entails God's lordship over people against the claim of lesser lords. Study Quran notes the wider rule that no community is punished before a messenger brings guidance, citing 28:59, 26:208, 6:131, 10:13, and 15:4."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q13", "question": "What grammatical analogies involving “هل” and neighboring forms appear in the cited discussions?", "turns_on": "The cited grammar chapter offers distinct analogies rather than one analysis of the verse; its explicit disagreement concerns whether من قدام is indefinite or definite and feminine.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q13/p1", "position": "Particle-like or ambiguous adverbial forms are restricted in declension and can have fixed vocalization.", "reasons": "Sībawayh lists أين، متى، كيف، حيث، إذ، إذا، قبل and بعد as ambiguous, non-fully-declinable adverbs, akin to interjections or non-nouns. قبل and بعد cannot freely stand like nouns and resemble particles across times; قبل، بعد and حيث take final ḍamma, though some analogize حيث to أين. He notes لدن's limited jussive behavior, its likeness to قط, and قط/حسب for ‘only’; لد abbreviates لدن, restored before pronouns, and resembles عن. Where two unvowelled consonants meet, the latter gets a vowel, but stays still after a vowel, as with هل، بل، أجل، نعم and جير. He also notes ḍamma following ḍamma in a form like رد يا فتى."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p2", "position": "Several comparison and place expressions shift between adverbial, nominal, adjectival, and elliptical uses.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl says مع takes accusative since معا is independent and pronoun constructions are adverbial. He treats من عل as more declinable; he and Sībawayh contrast أول and حكم with invariant الذي and من. Al-Khalīl reads أول in مذ عام أول as adjective with من عامك omitted, and also as a noun; أول من أمس and بعد غد omit comparisons. Sībawayh says ابدأ به أول omits من كذا, obligatory in عام أول. Al-Khalīl records rare adverbial مذ عام أول. Sībawayh makes أسفل an adverb in زيد أسفل منك, comparing 8:42, and comparative أفعل in جاء من أسفل, comparing 33:10. Al-Khalīl says دون، فوق، تحت، قبل، بعد accept complements and nominal uses; poetry attests من تحت، من عل، من أمامه and من دون. A poetic أولا can be adjective or adverb; al-Jaʿdī exemplifies accusative أماما and خلفا by analogy with يمنة and شأمة."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p3", "position": "من أمام and related bare place terms are indefinite unless attached to a definite noun.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl prefers this on Arab usage; Sībawayh cites ʿAlawiyyīn and Tamīmī forms من قديديمة and من وريئة, comparing صباحا and other time adverbs. Yūnus instead treats من قدام as definite and feminine diptote; Sībawayh says none of his Arab informants used that analysis."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p4", "position": "Yūnus treats من قدام as definite and feminine, hence diptote.", "reasons": "Sībawayh reports this to reject it against the Arab usage he consulted."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p5", "position": "When used as a personal name, these forms change shape like لو، هل، بل، ليت and ذا.", "reasons": "Sībawayh uses هل among the examples of forms adapted on naming."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p6", "position": "Poetic necessity can make معكم rhyme like هل.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites al-Rāʿī's verse."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p7", "position": "هل is also analyzed in the summons هلم, whose derivation and dialectal inflection are disputed.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān says هلم is an invitation. One derivation combines hā with lammamtu ‘I gathered or set right’ after dropping alif; another parses hal umm, ‘will you approach?’, linked to هل لك إلى. Hijaz leaves هلم unchanged in dual/plural, while Tamīm inflects it."}, {"id": "79:18/q13/p8", "position": "General rhetorical and syntactic examples show expressions used beyond their literal function.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān lists prepositions, commands, prohibitions, questions, wishes, hopes and calls as rhetorical forms. Al-Burhān records two other disputed analyses: for accompaniment waw, some make waw govern its object, while the preferred account lets the preceding verb govern through waw; for a verb joined to a verbal noun, Kūfans allow it, while the preferred account uses conjunction and implicit أن."}]}

Bint al-Shati connects direction to the straight path with the root's raised rock in water and daylight, both making a route clear. Abu Hayyan identifies the promised purification with guidance to oneness and knowledge. Biqai says the Lord teaches pleasing actions and blameworthy traits."}, {"id": "79:19/q01/p3", "position": "He directs Pharaoh toward God's approval and reward.", "reasons": "Tabrisi offers this as an alternative to teaching him to know his Creator and Sustainer; Ibn Ashur describes guidance as pointing along a path to a desired goal if the person accepts it."}, {"id": "79:19/q01/p4", "position": "Inwardly, guidance is knowledge of the unity of the divine Essence, softening and dissolving selfhood.", "reasons": "Qashani reads the preceding purification as annihilation of selfhood and this guidance to fear as knowledge of the Essence's unity."}]}
{"id": "79:19/q02", "question": "Is a human guide indispensable for knowing God?", "turns_on": "Whether Moses' offer makes a teacher a necessary condition for knowledge or shows the benefit of instruction and indication.", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q02/p1", "position": "Yes: knowledge of God must come through a guide, and this guidance is the mission's chief aim.", "reasons": "Razi reports proponents citing Moses' explicit offer of guidance as proof. {"id": "79:19/q03", "question": "Why does Moses call God 'your Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q03/p1", "position": "The familiar title gently presses God's lordship over Pharaoh and opens a path to monotheism and fear.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it could win a hearing without provoking Pharaoh, so faith may enter gradually after Moses' proof. {"id": "79:19/q04", "question": "What does 'then you will fear' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the fear is explained by religious conduct and punishment or by Qashani's inward account of divine unity and loss of selfhood.", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q04/p1", "position": "Pharaoh would fear God and His punishment, with reverence expressed in duties and avoidance of disobedience.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates khashya with khawf, fear. Nahhas specifies fear of punishment through avoiding disobedience. Wahidi's gloss adds salvation through fear and affirmation of oneness; the scholars of meaning specify performing required duties from fear of punishment. Tabrisi adds leaving prohibited acts; Baydawi and Biqai add both duties and prohibitions. Elmalili specifies reverent fear of wrath and punishment. Ibn Ashur says religious usage means fear of God and the verb is intransitive here because God is its understood object. Tabatabai's reported repentance reading makes this faith-driven fear motivate obedience and restrain sin."}, {"id": "79:19/q04/p2", "position": "Inwardly, fear is knowledge of divine unity that softens and dissolves selfhood.", "reasons": "Qashani links it with the preceding purification understood as annihilation of selfhood."}]}
{"id": "79:19/q05", "question": "Why does fear follow guidance?", "turns_on": "Whether the explanation emphasizes knowledge as fear's cause, Pharaoh's acceptance of guidance, or an inward transformation.", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q05/p1", "position": "Knowledge of God gained through guidance produces reverent fear, which then grounds obedience and good action.", "reasons": "Sulami reports Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi calling fear the fruit of sound guidance. Ibn Atiyya places knowledge after guidance and fear after knowledge, citing 35:28. Razi says guidance precedes fear and knowledge precedes obedience, citing 16:2 and 20:14; he also cites 35:28. Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Alusi, Ibn Ashur, and Tabatabai also invoke 35:28, that the learned fear God. Nasafi reports a sage saying one who knows God cannot disobey Him even for an instant. Elmalili says lack of knowledge leaves one without reverence or moral guard and leads to wrongdoing. Bint al-Shati says fear requires faith in one's Lord. Bursevi frames knowledge as adornment following purification as cleansing. Ibn Ashur reports al-Wasiti's successive stages: the beginning of knowledge is fear, followed by reverence, glorification, awe, and finally annihilation."}, {"id": "79:19/q05/p2", "position": "Fear follows if Pharaoh accepts the offered guidance and its path to the goal.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur conditions the sequence on Pharaoh's readiness for purification and says guidance points to the goal only if the guided person accepts it; the order of clauses follows the order of events."}, {"id": "79:19/q05/p3", "position": "Inward knowledge of the divine Essence's unity yields fear by softening and dissolving selfhood.", "reasons": "Qashani connects the guidance to fear with annihilation of selfhood in purification."}]}
{"id": "79:19/q06", "question": "What conduct or outcome does fear produce?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q06/p1", "position": "It motivates duties and every good while restraining disobedience and evil; feeling secure emboldens wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Tabrisi specify avoiding disobedience and prohibitions.
